lesson.text: Quick memory: what does democracy mean? (Rule by the people.) While Athens tried democracy, a small town in Italy was growing: Rome. Today: how Rome grew from one town into a huge empire, and how it was ruled.

The Romans told a legend: twins called Romulus and Remus, raised by a she-wolf, founded Rome in 753 BC. At first kings ruled. In 509 BC, the Romans drove out their last king and chose never to have another.

They made a republic, from res publica, 'the people's thing'. Each year the citizens elected two consuls to lead, so no one person held all the power. The Senate, a council of experienced men, gave advice and ran money and wars.

Rich families, the patricians, and ordinary citizens, the plebeians, argued over power. The plebeians won their own leaders, called tribunes. About 450 BC, Rome's laws were written on twelve tablets for everyone to see.

Rome's army conquered Italy, then fought Carthage in North Africa on and off for over 100 years. The Carthaginian general Hannibal even crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BC, but Rome won in the end.

Then rich generals fought each other for power. Julius Caesar made himself ruler for life and was killed by senators in 44 BC. His adopted son Octavian won the wars that followed, and in 27 BC he became Augustus, the first emperor.

At its biggest, in AD 117, the empire stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Iraq. In AD 395 it split in two. The west ended in AD 476: from 27 BC, that is 27 + 476 − 1 = 502 years of emperors.
Try it in the world: build a Senate house with rows of benches, and elect two consuls among your friends for one game day. Next: life in Roman times.

choices: a state whose citizens elect their leaders
a state ruled by a king
exercises.explain: In a republic, citizens elect leaders for a time, instead of having a king.

exercises.prompt: The legend says Rome was founded by twins raised by a she-wolf.
exercises.explain: True: the legend of Romulus and Remus. It is a story, not history we can check.

exercises.prompt: How many consuls were elected each year?
exercises.hint: Rome did not want one person to hold all the power.
exercises.explain: Two consuls, so each could stop the other.

exercises.prompt: Who was the first Roman emperor?
exercises.hint: He took a new name in 27 BC.
exercises.explain: Augustus, once called Octavian, from 27 BC.

exercises.prompt: Julius Caesar was the first Roman emperor.
exercises.hint: What happened in 44 BC, and in 27 BC?
exercises.explain: False: Caesar ruled for life but was killed in 44 BC; Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order, earliest first.
exercises.hint: BC years count down: the bigger the number, the longer ago.
items: Rome is founded, says the legend (753 BC)

exercises.prompt: Why did Rome have two consuls instead of one?
exercises.hint: What had the Romans disliked about their kings?
choices: so no one person held all the power
one for summer, one for winter
to lead two armies to Egypt
exercises.explain: Two consuls, each able to stop the other, meant no one person held all the power.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Which did the plebeians win? Which lasted only a year?
exercises.explain: Consul: a yearly leader. Senate: the council. Tribune: the plebeians' leader. Emperor: a ruler with total power.

exercises.prompt: Rome became a republic in 509 BC and Augustus became emperor in 27 BC. How many years did the republic last?
exercises.hint: Both years are BC, so they count down: take the smaller number from the bigger one.
He brought elephants over the mountains.
choices: a general from Carthage who crossed the Alps
exercises.explain: Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BC.

exercises.prompt: Augustus became emperor in 27 BC. The western empire ended in AD 476. How many years is that? Remember: there is no year 0.
exercises.hint: Count the years up to AD 1, then the years after it.
exercises.explain: From 27 BC to AD 1 is 27 years; from AD 1 to AD 476 is 475 more. 27 + 475 = 502 years.

exercises.prompt: Why were Rome's laws written on tablets for everyone to see?
exercises.hint: Before, who decided what the law said?
choices: so everyone knew the same rules
so only the rich could read them
exercises.explain: Written laws meant everyone could know them, and they were the same for all.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: the republic or the empire?
items: the western half ends in AD 476
exercises.hint: The republic lasted from 509 BC to 27 BC; then came the emperors.
exercises.explain: Republic: yearly consuls, Hannibal in 218 BC. Empire: Augustus, Hadrian's Wall, and the end of the west in AD 476.

exercises.prompt: What was one reason the republic ended?
exercises.hint: Think of Julius Caesar and Octavian.
choices: rich generals fought each other for power
exercises.explain: Generals with their own armies fought for power, until Octavian became Augustus, the first emperor.

exercises.prompt: At its biggest, the Roman Empire reached from Britain to Egypt.
exercises.explain: True: in AD 117 it stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Iraq.
